transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-06-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE); Liam Chen (Redwood SE); Evan Ross (CTO - Harborwell); Priya Menon (VP Eng); Diego Alvarez (ML Platform)

Summary (auto):
Harborwell is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted + dedicated and an eventual private on-prem path for latency-sensitive streaming inference. Primary goals: p95 latency under 250ms for short-form responses (<=128 tokens), predictable throughput for 500 concurrent streaming sessions, and a fallback strategy that preserves availability during spikes. Security and auditability (SOC2, KMS, SSO) are must-haves. Next steps: bench template, security pack, schedule dry-run.

Topics:
- p95 targets and how measured (streaming vs non-streaming)
- concurrency modeling and token/sec benchmarks
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs (latency, cost, isolation)
- KV/prefix cache, batching, quantization impact
- Security posture: SOC 2, SSO, KMS/HSM, network diagram

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): ok, everybody, thanks for joining. we got about 55 minutes. quick intros?
[00:08] Evan (Harborwell CTO): hi all, im Evan. we run harborwell's inference infra and platform, want to understand hosting paths for low latency streaming.
[00:14] Priya (VP Eng): Priya here, delivery timelines, securing infra and procurement constraints.
[00:19] Diego (ML Platform): Diego, I own model infra and perf, I'll share traces after this call.
[00:25] Liam (Redwood SE): Liam from Redwood, I'll dig into throughput numbers and sketch out test plan. quick note — apologies if our transcript messes up product names, sometimes it writes Redwood Dedicate instead of Dedicated, ha.
[00:35] Evan: ha, been there. ok core ask - p95 under 250ms streaming for 128 token answers, 500 concurrent streams, spikes to 2k for 5 mins. cost is a factor but SLOs non-negotiable.
[00:48] Maya: got it. couple clarifying q's: is the 250ms p95 measured from client to client (end-to-end) or just server side token emission?
[00:57] Diego: mostly server-side plus network within our VPC — so includes routing inside our infra but not the user's home network.
[01:04] Priya: our clients are enterprise customers, two regions (us-west, eu-west) — data residency for eu needs routing.
[01:12] Liam: good. two dimensions: latency per token (streaming) and tail under concurrency. streaming tends to expose p95 due to scheduling and batching. are you currently using batching or KV caching?
[01:21] Diego: KV cache yes for chat contexts, but we need prefix caching too for repeated patterns. batching is minimal because we stream; we avoid artificial batching to keep latency low.
[01:31] Mia? (Speaker 5): [inaudible]
[01:34] Maya: cool. for hosting modes: short primer — Hosted API gives fastest time to value (Redwood handles infra), Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput and latency, Private gives you a customer-managed control plane and on-prem option. each has different cost/latency tradeoffs.
[01:52] Evan: can you quantify typical p95 numbers for streaming 128 tokens on Hosted vs Dedicated? rough ballpark.
[01:58] Liam: ballpark — on our hosted fleet with optimized kernels for 8k context models, streaming p95 for ~100-150 tokens is often 180-320ms depending on model and sequence length distribution. Dedicated can tighten that often to 130-240ms because of reserved CUDA warm pools and less multi-tenancy jitter. Private may get lower if you put it on the right GPUs and networking — but it depends on your on-prem network and HSM latencies.
[02:22] Priya: that's helpful, but the 180-320 range is wide. what moves it?
[02:27] Liam: sequence length variance (longer sequences increases per-token time), model variant (quantized vs fp16), continuous batching when many low-latency reqs arrive in a microburst, and KV cache hit rates. also kernel selection and tokenizer overhead.
[02:40] Evan: you mentioned quantization — we plan int8 for cost. any p95 downside?
[02:45] Liam: good question. int8 typically increases throughput and reduces latency slightly due to smaller memory footprints, but model-specific quality regressions can happen; Redwood Optimize suggests quant profiles per workload. and sometimes int8 kernels have different tail characteristics depending on HBM contention.
[03:00] Diego: about concurrency modeling — we have 500 steady streams, each ~1 token/sec on average but bursts to 10 tokens/sec during active typing. we need to size for bursty token/sec and maintain p95.
[03:12] Liam: ok, so steady-state token rate ~500 tokens/sec, burst up to 5k tokens/sec. helpful if you can share sample traffic traces — Diego said you'll provide.
[03:22] Diego: yes will upload post call.
[03:25] Maya: action item — Diego to share traces (we captured that).
[03:29] Evan: also interested in fallback strategy — if dedicated capacity saturates, what's the path?
[03:34] Liam: we can set routing policies — overflow to compatible model variants or hosted pool; we call it smart routing and graceful degradation. you can also set automatic fallback to a lower-cost but higher-latency variant, or to cached responses for repeated queries.
[03:48] Priya: any multi-region failover overhead? we prefer local region for latency but fall back to another region on outage.
[03:55] Liam: cross-region adds network RTT; Redwood can do regional routing with automatic fallback; we recommend multi-region warm pools for <250ms p95 across regions but that increases cost.
[04:06] Evan: security — we need SOC 2, SSO (SAML), RBAC, and KMS integration. is that covered on Hosted?
[04:12] Maya: Hosted supports SOC 2 (we'll share certs), SSO/SAML, RBAC, and customer-managed KMS in Dedicated/Private; Hosted can support keys via envelope encryption patterns and bring-your-own-key in select enterprise tiers. we'll send the security pack.
[04:25] Diego: and audit logs? must keep full per-request logs for 12 months for compliance.
[04:30] Liam: audit logs are supported; retention tiers are an add-on with longer retention. Private gives you full control of log retention.
[04:36] Evan: great. can you walk through the recommended bench test to validate p95 under our burst model?
[04:42] Liam: sure. we'll provide a benchmark template — core pieces: reproducer script that replays your traces, param for concurrency sessions, token/sec distribution, and streaming vs non-streaming modes. measure server-side emission time and end-to-end in VPC. recommended to run three phases: 1) steady-state warm-up 30m, 2) spike tests ramp x4 for 10m windows, 3) sustained load to verify autoscale.
[05:03] Priya: what's the expected noise floor for our tests? we want confidence intervals.
[05:07] Liam: run multiple runs, collect p50/p95/p99; include kernel warm vs cold starts. we'll help interpret.
[05:13] Evan: cost — can you give rough cost delta hosted vs dedicated?
[05:16] Maya: rough: dedicated has higher fixed committed cost but lower variable per-token costs due to utilization. hosted is pay-as-you-go with slightly higher per-token rates. we'll provide a modeled spreadsheet after we get your traffic traces.
[05:29] Speaker 5 (inaudible): [mumbled]
[05:32] Diego: another technical nuance — we use long context occasionally (4k sequences) and short in most traffic; how does Redwood handle mixed seqlen?
[05:40] Liam: runtime chooses kernels per sequence length and can colocate workloads, but mixed seqlen can increase tail. we recommend seqlen-aware routing or dedicated pools per seqlen band to keep p95 tighter.
[05:51] Evan: do you support KV cache persistence across sessions?
[05:55] Liam: we have prefix/KV caching that can be shared and TTLed; caching reduces token compute and improves p95 for repeated contexts. cache misses still hit model.
[06:03] Priya: we plan to start with hosted for dev and a small prod slice on dedicated, then private pilot. timeline Q: can Redwood support an on-prem dry-run in 3 weeks?
[06:12] Maya: depends on infra but we can schedule a 1-hr dry-run. Liam will prepare a test plan.
[06:18] Liam: yes, we can do a dry-run. need your infra contact for networking and access; also need sample traces and an image of the model you run (or model name).
[06:28] Evan: we'll share that.
[06:30] [Timestamp jump]
[20:05] Liam: quick aside — regarding quantization, we saw some customers get unexpected knob interactions: int8 + aggressive batching increased p95 tail in certain GPUs due to memory thrash. so testing specific to your model is critical.
[20:19] Priya: good to know.
[20:23] Evan: about SLOs — if a p95 breach occurs, what tooling do you expose to debug?
[20:27] Liam: Console has per-token latency breakdown, token-level charts, per-route/traces and sampler for stack traces; can hook your tracing to our tracing hooks. we also provide canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies.
[20:39] Diego: any recommended hardware for private pilot? A100s? H100?
[20:44] Liam: H100s give best throughput for large models; A100 good for many models too. for streaming and tail, H100 often reduces per-token latency but cost more. we'll include recommended instance types in our follow-up.
[20:56] Priya: and networking — we need <5ms intra-cluster jitter.
[21:00] Liam: that is doable with proper NICs and RDMA; if on cloud, use placement groups and local zones.
[21:06] Evan: can Dedicated guarantee isolation for noisy neighbor?
[21:10] Maya: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools that avoid multi-tenant noisy neighbors; Dedicated also supports burst capacity against hosted for temporary surges.
[21:19] Diego: curious about autoscale — how fast can you scale on Dedicated?
[21:23] Liam: autoscale depends on capacity buffer and pre-warmed instances; we can do sub-minute scale up with pre-warmed nodes, but cold provisioning takes longer. recommended to keep burst buffer for expected spikes.
[21:35] Evan: if we overflow to hosted, do we retain cryptographic separation?
[21:40] Maya: yes, data in transit is encrypted; we have contract terms and access controls. for some customers, they require Private for strict separation.
[21:48] Priya: timeline — we want a pilot in 6 weeks and a production cutover in 3 months if tests pass. any blockers?
[21:55] Maya: main blockers are security sign-off and the dry-run results. procurement and network access for dry-run usually take the most time.
[22:03] Evan: ok. Diego will assemble traces and we'll need Liam's throughput estimates for 500/2k concurrency.
[22:09] Liam: noted. I'll produce three scenarios: steady (500), burst (2k), and pessimistic (4k).
[22:14] [Short crosstalk]
[30:00] Liam: another note on metrics — measure server emission time per token, that's the important signal for streaming p95. also measure cold start percent.
[30:10] Diego: will add cold starts to traces.
[30:14] Priya: procurement question — are there minimum commitment periods for Dedicated?
[30:20] Maya: Dedicated usually has monthly or annual commitments; specifics depend on capacity and negotiated terms. we'll share a sample contract and pricing sheet.
[30:30] Evan: any reference customers in our domain? low-latency streaming for enterprise search?
[30:36] Maya: we can share anonymized case studies; will include a couple in the follow up.
[30:41] Priya: concerns about auditability — need per-token provenance attached to logs for regulated workflows.
[30:47] Liam: we can attach request ids and model-version metadata to each token event and export to your SIEM. retention configurable.
[30:56] Evan: last technical: how does Redwood handle quantized model rollbacks if quality regresses?
[31:02] Liam: rollouts include canary and automatic rollback based on eval metrics tied to your prompt sets; Redwood Optimize will flag quality regressions.
[31:12] Diego: good.
[31:15] [Wrap-up]
[31:18] Maya: recap — Diego shares traces and model names; Maya sends benchmark template, pricing and SOC2/security pack; Liam prepares throughput estimates and test plan; schedule dry-run next week (Tues preferred).
[31:32] Evan: sounds good.
[31:35] Priya: thanks everyone.
[31:38] Maya: thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invite.
[31:41] [End of recording: 15:55 UTC]
